tone_statements.citation: Hölzl, Andreas. 2021. Longjia (China) – Language Contexts. Language Documentation and Description 20, 13-34. DOI 10.25894/LDD29 (CC BY-NC).
tone_statements.quote: Western Guizhou is a mountainous region characterized by humid subtropical highland climate in the northern periphery of the Mainland Southeast Asian area. Longjia shares many features with the languages of this area (e.g., a tone system: Pojiao 55, 33, 13, 31), although its typology and areal connections have yet to be explored.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the 23-page article (a full-text search for stress/accent/syllab: no hits). Only prosodic remark, p. 24 (sec. 6 'Linguistic ecology'): 'Longjia shares many features with the languages of this area (e.g., a tone system: Pojiao 55, 33, 13, 31), although its typology and areal connections have yet to be explored.' Sec. 7 (pp. 25-30) gives tone-numbered examples (prenasalized onsets, pronouns, numerals) from Zhang & Li's 1982 Pojiao field notes and states the only description is GMSWSB 1982: 22-43; 'Typological and historical descriptions of the language wi…

tone.quote: Western Guizhou is a mountainous region characterized by humid subtropical highland climate in the northern periphery of the Mainland Southeast Asian area. Longjia shares many features with the languages of this area (e.g., a tone system: Pojiao 55, 33, 13, 31), although its typology and areal connections have yet to be explored.
tone.locator: p. 24, sec. 6 'Linguistic ecology'; cf. Hölzl 2026 sec. 2.6.3 p. 32: '4 in Dafang Longjia (cf. Zhang & Li 1982)'
tone.says: Four tones in the Dafang (Pojiao) variety, cited as 55, 33, 13, 31 (two level, one rising, one falling); tone sandhi not yet understood. Extinct; tone values rest on 1982 fieldnotes by Zhang & Li.

sources.citation: Hsiu, Andrew. 2013. New endangered Tibeto-Burman languages of southwestern China: Mondzish, Longjia, Pherbu, and others. Paper presented at ICSTLL 46, Dartmouth College, 8-10 Aug 2013. 24 slides. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1127796.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone. Longjia slides (sec. 3): extinct in the 1970s/80s; ~20 words/phrases written in Chinese characters by Zhao Qiming in 1974 (Jiangyizhai, Anshun); cognate percentages quoted from the 2002 Guizhou Ethnic Gazetteer; a 7-item comparison with Caijia and Bai (Longjia forms given without tone marks); 'Longjia is too poorly attested to classify with certainty.' Zenodo could not be reached by automated download by automated download; downloaded via direct download and copied into the custody folder.

sources.citation: Hsiu, Andrew. Longjia page, 'Sino-Tibetan languages' section of msealangs (sites.google.com/site/msealangs/sino-tibetan/languages), fieldwork notes 2013.
sources.note: No linguistic data: reports that the last fluent speakers most likely died in the 1970s, a 99-year-old semi-speaker in Sanjin (Zhijin) had recently died, and that a local researcher Yang Dehua's IPA notes of 'a few hundred Longjia words' are lost.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Longjia language' (accessed 2026-09-17), citing Guizhou Province Gazetteer: Ethnic Gazetteer (贵州省志·民族志, 2002) and Hölzl 2021.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Reports '38 onsets and 22 rimes (8 simple, 14 complex)' and 'many prenasalized onsets' (attributed to the 2002 Gazetteer); four varieties Pojiao (Dafang), Huaxi (Qianxi), Jiangyizhai (Puding), Caiguan (Anshun).

sources.note: States that Dafang Longjia has a (complex) tone system of 4 tones (cf. Zhang & Li 1982), Hezhang Caijia 4 or 5, Lujia at least 4, 'not including sandhi phenomena that mostly remain unclear for now', and lists 'morphological tone changes that remain to be investigated in detail' as a shared Ta-Li/MSEA feature; sec. 2.6.2 adds tone-transcribed Longjia forms from five independent records (e.g. 'to eat' wa33 1950s, wa31 1982/2004/1989) and regular correspondences between recordings; announces a forthcoming grammar of Longjia with all materials.

sources.citation: Hölzl, Andreas. 2022. A typological profile of Longjia, an archaic Sinitic language. Paper presented at the 14th Conference of the Association for Linguistic Typology (ALT 14), University of Texas at Austin, 15-17 December 2022. (Copy uploaded to Academia.edu, item 93113627.)

sources.access_detail: online with restricted access (login, paywall or limited view)
sources.note: Snippet (web-search summary of the Academia copy): Longjia has 'tonal distinctions with phonemic relevance' alongside a rich vowel inventory and isolating morphology, and 'uses tone as a morphological device, exemplified by syntactic tone changes such as wa31 (to eat) and wa55 po55 (to eat dinner)' -- i.e. first-hand typological sketch with a tone paragraph and a note on morphological/sandhi tone change.

sources.note: Record (Hölzl 2026: 30-31, read; Hölzl 2021: 30 on the CGZZ copy, read): pp. 116-119 record the Longjia ('Bai') of Anshun; the 2004 copy of it is 'a brief presentation of the phonology, a couple of lexical items, and a few expressions' in tone-numbered transcription (e.g. wa31 'to eat', Wu 1989: 117; CGZZ ts'wn42 'person', t'o55 'coal'), with fewer typographic errors in the 1989 original; the tone inventory it lists has not been seen.
